query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In HfNbTaTiZr, mismatched thermal expansion among the constituent elements generates local stress concentrations that couple with dislocation-mediated plasticity. As temperature changes, these local internal stresses modify dislocation interactions and slip pathways, causing the anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior observed across cold-rolled, aged, and high-temperature creep conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, nominally equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy in as-cast or solution-annealed condition, exhibiting a predominantly BCC solid solution with minimal second phases.
generation.intervention: Conduct in situ high-temperature mechanical loading from room temperature to ~1250°C while simultaneously measuring thermal expansion (e.g., via dilatometry or X-ray/ neutron diffraction) and lattice strain evolution under controlled stress levels. Parallel tests can vary strain rate or incorporate a slight compositional tweak (e.g., reduced Hf or Zr) to alter thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.conditions: Isothermal holds at selected temperatures (25°C, ~600–800°C, ~1250°C) combined with ramp profiles, each under constant stress or strain rate, in an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Local stress fields arising from thermal expansion mismatch between different constituent atoms, along with minor atomic clustering or short-range ordering, which influence dislocation motion and slip activity.
generation.mechanism: Elevated local internal stresses form upon heating or cooling due to elemental expansion differences. These stresses impede or redirect dislocation glide, causing unusual hardening or brittleness plateaus in specific temperature regimes.
generation.predicted_outcome: As the temperature increases, distinctive changes in flow stress and work-hardening behavior will track with measured internal stress shifts from thermal expansion mismatch. Compositions with larger mismatch (e.g., higher Hf fraction) will show more pronounced and earlier onset of the strength/ductility anomalies than compositions with smaller mismatch.
generation.baseline: Tests performed isothermally without simultaneous thermal expansion measurements or with narrower temperature windows, which lack the steep variations in internal stress attributable to thermal mismatch.
generation.boundary: Below ~300°C, dislocation slip is dominated by standard lattice friction with minimal mismatch-induced stresses; above ~1250°C, creep mechanisms dominate and overshadow mismatch effects, causing the phenomenon to fade.
generation.uncertainty: Whether local atomic ordering or minor nanoscale precipitates are necessary to stabilize mismatch-induced stresses remains unclear. Alternatively, small changes in composition or local structure could shift thermal expansion and obscure the role of mismatch in mechanical response.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare standard HfNbTaTiZr coupons with composition-modified variants that reduce the difference in element-specific thermal expansions. Conduct the same in situ high-temperature mechanical tests and track lattice expansion and yield behavior for each composition.
measurements: Thermal expansion coefficient extracted from in situ diffraction or dilatometry
Macroscopic flow stress and strain to failure under temperature ramps
Lattice strains with crystallographic texture analysis to detect local stress distributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If varying the thermal expansion mismatch (via composition changes) does not produce systematic shifts in internal stresses or observable changes in stress–strain anomalies, then local mismatch stress cannot be the primary driver of the anomalous mechanical and thermoelastic behavior, falsifying the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

Compared with the strength, the plasticity change of the alloy was more complex, as presented in Figure 4b. Theoretically, with the increase in the temperature, the dislocation movement becomes easier due to the decrease in the resistance to the dislocation movement and the increase in the dislocation movement mode, and the elongation at the fracture of the single-phase alloys increases [,,]. However, in this study, a low-plasticity plateau appeared when the temperature was between 873 K and 1073 K. In other words, in that temperature range, the alloy became more brittle compared to that at room temperature. Figure 6 shows the fracture diagram of the sample after tensile testing at 673, 873, and 1073 K. The specimens exhibited a ductile fracture at all three temperatures, and obvious dimples and fluvial patterns were observed from the fracture surface []. It is obvious from the figure that there is little difference between the fractures at all three temperatures. In addition, obvious black spots can be seen in all three images, which is the residue of the alloy oxidation. These oxides also show that the alloy was slightly oxidized during the tensile tests at high temperature.

cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations. occupying_moves.lever: Systematically control temperature and loading paths to track both stress–strain and thermal expansion responses
occupying_moves.technique: In situ high-temperature mechanical testing coupled with high-energy diffraction and thermomechanical analysis; crystal plasticity or finite-element simulation to capture thermo-mechanical coupling
occupying_moves.conditions: Broad thermal range (e.g., from room temperature to 1250 °C) under varying strain rates and controlled atmosphere

occupying_moves.lever: Manipulate thermal expansion mismatch by adjusting compositional or reinforcement factors
occupying_moves.technique: Differential thermal analysis and mechanical characterization (tensile and hardness tests), performed on systematically varied compositional or multiphase samples
occupying_moves.conditions: Solidification under different cooling/heating protocols, measuring resultant microstructure, thermal stresses, and strength at high temperature

chosen.lever: Temperature and loading path control to reveal synergy of thermal expansion and mechanical deformation
chosen.technique: In situ high-temperature tensile tests with simultaneous thermal expansion measurements, complemented by crystal plasticity modeling
chosen.conditions: Continuous temperature ramping from ~25 to 1250 °C under controlled strain rates and atmosphere
chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the missing unification of stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior by measuring and modeling mechanical response and thermal expansion together across service-relevant temperatures, thereby testing the hypothesis that thermoelastic and thermal expansion effects govern the observed mechanical inconsistencies.
